svg.text: PowerMonger: everything the game does in one simulation step (a tick), in order
The drawing calls sit behind a divider that sets how often the screen is redrawn; at normal speed it is 1, so everything runs every tick
PowerMonger (Bullfrog / Electronic Arts, 1990, here the Atari ST version) is a war game on a height-mapped land of settlements: the player
gives orders to captains, the computer lords give orders through the same path, and every man carries them out on his own. This figure
comes from reverse-engineering the game's 68000 machine code (the ST's CPU) and running it in an emulator. The game advances in ticks.
Each tick runs one routine ($13000) that moves the whole world one step: the commander AI decides, every man, boat and building takes one
step of its own small state machine, and the screen is redrawn.
The figure shows one tick. Left: the calls $13000 makes, in order. Right: the loop $14b62 that walks every object record once and jumps to
the handler for its current mode. Lower right: the other data pools the same tick moves. The point to take away is that there is no
separate AI per unit type (observed in every record traced, not proven absent): a record holds a mode number (one byte saying what that
man or boat is doing), the loop runs that mode's handler, and the handler's choice of the next mode is the behaviour.
$ numbers are addresses in the game's memory, given as citations; the text says what each one is. Evidence: proven = checked against the game's own code with
a match count; observed = seen in the running game; inferred = read from the code or reasoned, not run.

g.text: if no game is running ($14e4e == 0), skip to $13058
commander AI: the computer lords decide orders
the smaller pools: animals, pigeons, arrows, forest
wait for the screen refresh (VBL), flush buffer $12ce0
ENTITY LOOP: steps every man, boat, house (right)
order executor: order slots $58016 -> group state
force ratio from the troop totals (0..4, $57fce)
The smaller-pools call ($3e06) also runs, per tick:
The entity loop ($14b62): one pass over every record per tick
object records: 512 slots of 50 bytes ($32) from $51b66;
read byte 5 of the record, the owner ($14b72)
read the position x, y (bytes 8, 10) and the mode (byte 31);
jump through a table of 75 handlers ($14bb4, entries $00..$94)
run one tick of that mode's handler (code $14c48..$1620e)
epilogue ($161c4): clamp the position, veto a step onto water (mode $00), relink
(relink = refile the record in its map-cell bucket); $16202 clamp + relink;
$16228 relink only; $1622c no write-back; then next record (+50 bytes, to $57f66)
What else moves each tick: the other data pools
The bucket chains link all pools by offsets from $51b66 (negative below it).

svg.text: How to read each panel
The tick (left)
Each row is one call made by $13000, top to bottom
in the order it runs: the routine's address, what
it does, and a fill for the evidence (key above).
The two purple italic lines are not calls; they
mark where the drawing block behind the divider
starts and ends.
Takeaway: the game's decisions (commander AI
$6522, entity loop $14b62, order executor $6a3a)
run on every tick. Only the four drawing calls
$1870, $12ce0, $178ae and $f898 sit behind the
divider, which is a drawing rate, not a simulation
rate: slowing the drawing does not slow the world,
and at normal speed the divider is 1 anyway.
The entity loop (right)
A flowchart for one record; the arrow on the right
goes back for the next record until the end of the
array. Byte 5 is the owner: 0 is a free slot,
negative a dying man, positive a live one. A live
record's mode (byte 31) indexes a table of 75
handler offsets at $14bb4.
Takeaway: one jump table replaces any per-type
logic. The handler moves the record one tick and
usually writes a new mode; the epilogue clamps the
position, vetoes a step onto water by setting mode
$00, and relinks the record into its map-cell
bucket.
The pools (lower right)
One row per data pool: what it holds, its base
address and record size, and the routine that
moves it each tick. "511 x 50 B" means 511 records
of 50 bytes.
Takeaway: only men, boats, buildings and markers
are object records. Animals, pigeons, arrows and
trees are smaller pools moved near the top of the
tick. The cell buckets let a man find neighbours
by walking one chain instead of scanning all 511
records.
Numbers and how we know them
Cadence, from a 3-million-instruction trace of mission 1: 13 ticks per 250 VBLs (screen refreshes: the ST's screen interrupt, one per displayed
frame), about 2.6 ticks a second; one tick takes as long as about 19 screen refreshes, so the game is limited by computation, not by the display.
$6522, $d322, $3e06 and $6a3a ran 13 times each in that trace, $14b62 14 times. One tick is about 200k to 230k emulated instructions ("steps").
A man, boat, building or marker is one 50-byte record and runs its mode handler once per tick inside $14b62. Animals, pigeons, arrows and trees are
separate pools moved by $3e06 near the top of the same tick; they are not entity records. Mission 1, settled view: about 50 of the 511 slots are in
use and about 26 reach a handler each tick.
Proven means checked against the game's own code: a Python rewrite of the routine was run beside the game's own 68000 code, called in isolation from
many saved game states (the emulator's callcap command), and every changed byte matched; "675/675" is matching bytes out of bytes compared. Proven
here: the $14b62 prologue and epilogues (675/675 and 1335/1335 tracked bytes), the dying path $1623c 275/275, animals and pigeons 45094/45094, arrows
4210/4210, the forest animator $4342 8 of 9 branches. Observed: the trace counts above. Inferred: the call-order listing, read from the disassembly.
Evidence:
proven (checked against the game's own code)
observed (seen in the running game)
inferred (read from the code, not run)
Sources: strategy.md "Where it runs", "Where the calls sit" and "Measured cadence"; ai.md "The simulation tick" and "The iterator"; generator py/fsm/build_tick.py; line-by-line
sources in tick.facts.md.
